explanation.exam_pattern: Active-active = both nodes work and share load (more capacity); active-passive = standby idle until failover.

questions.stem: A client must resolve a hostname to an IPv6 address. Which DNS record type returns that answer?

explanation.correct: The AAAA ('quad-A') record maps a hostname to a 128-bit IPv6 address.

distractors.A: A PTR record is used for reverse lookups (IP address back to a name).
distractors.B: An A record maps a hostname to a 32-bit IPv4 address, not IPv6.
distractors.D: A CNAME is an alias pointing to another canonical name; it returns no address itself.

explanation.exam_pattern: A = IPv4, AAAA = IPv6, PTR = reverse lookup, CNAME = alias.

questions.stem: An administrator wants a specific network printer to ALWAYS receive the same IP address from DHCP, tied to its MAC address, while still being managed by the DHCP server. Which configuration achieves this?

explanation.correct: A reservation binds a chosen IP to the device's MAC in the DHCP scope, so DHCP always hands that host the same address while still managing it centrally.

distractors.A: An IP helper forwards DHCP requests across subnets; it does not reserve an address.
distractors.C: An exclusion removes addresses from the pool so DHCP never assigns them; you would then have to static-assign the printer manually.
distractors.D: A shorter lease just renews more often; it does not pin a specific address to the host.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reservation = DHCP always gives a set IP to a MAC; exclusion = addresses DHCP must NOT assign.

questions.stem: Clients on VLAN 20 receive no address from the central DHCP server on VLAN 10 because their broadcast Discover never leaves the local subnet. Which configuration on the VLAN 20 gateway resolves this?

options.text: A DHCP exclusion range on VLAN 20
An IP helper-address (DHCP relay) pointing to the DHCP server

explanation.correct: Routers do not forward broadcasts, so a DHCP relay / IP helper-address on the client-side gateway converts the broadcast Discover to a unicast and forwards it to the server across subnets.

distractors.A: Lease duration has no effect on whether requests reach the server across subnets.
distractors.B: DHCP snooping is a security filter against rogue DHCP servers; it does not relay Discover messages.
distractors.C: An exclusion merely withholds some addresses; it does not forward cross-subnet DHCP requests.

explanation.exam_pattern: DHCP broadcast can't cross a router → configure IP helper-address (DHCP relay) on the client's gateway.

questions.stem: A workstation sends a query to its configured DNS server, which then performs the full lookup on the client's behalf — querying root, TLD, and other servers until it returns the final answer and caches it. In this exchange the client's DNS server is acting as what?

explanation.correct: A recursive resolver does the full legwork for the client (root → TLD → authoritative), returns the final answer, and caches it. The client itself makes only one (recursive) request.

distractors.A: An authoritative server holds and answers only for its own zone data; it does not chase the whole chain for clients.
distractors.C: Root hints are the preconfigured addresses of the root servers a resolver starts from, not a role the server plays.
distractors.D: A reverse-lookup zone maps IP addresses to names (PTR); it is a zone type, not this resolving behavior.

explanation.exam_pattern: Recursive resolver does the work (root→TLD→authoritative) and caches; authoritative answers only for its own zone.

questions.stem: An organization wants assurance that DNS responses are authentic and have not been forged or tampered with, using cryptographic signatures on the records. Which technology provides this?

explanation.correct: DNSSEC digitally signs DNS records (RRSIG/DNSKEY/DS) so resolvers can validate that answers are authentic and unmodified, defeating spoofing/cache poisoning. Note it validates, it does not encrypt.

distractors.B: DHCP lease length is unrelated to DNS record authenticity.
distractors.C: Chaining CNAMEs is only aliasing; it adds no authentication or integrity check.
distractors.D: Split-horizon serves different answers to internal vs external clients but does not cryptographically sign or validate records.

explanation.exam_pattern: DNSSEC = signatures that validate record authenticity/integrity (not confidentiality — DoH/DoT handle encryption).

questions.stem: A security review requires that all SNMP management traffic be both authenticated AND encrypted. Which SNMP version must be deployed to meet this requirement?

options.text: SNMPv2c with a long community string

explanation.correct: Only SNMPv3 adds a security model with authentication (authNoPriv) and optional privacy/encryption (authPriv); it is the version required when SNMP must be authenticated and encrypted.

distractors.B: SNMPv2c relies on a cleartext community string — no real authentication framework and no encryption.
distractors.C: SNMPv1 is the oldest version, also community-based and sent in cleartext.
distractors.D: Lengthening a community string does not add authentication or encryption; it is still cleartext v2c.

explanation.exam_pattern: Authentication + encryption for SNMP = SNMPv3 (authPriv); v1/v2c use cleartext community strings.

questions.stem: An administrator wants managed devices to IMMEDIATELY notify the SNMP manager the moment an interface goes down, instead of waiting for the next scheduled query. Which SNMP mechanism provides this?

explanation.correct: A trap (or inform) is an unsolicited, agent-initiated message pushed to the manager the instant an event occurs, so notification is immediate rather than waiting for the next poll.

distractors.A: Polling is the manager querying agents on a schedule, so a failure is not seen until the next poll interval.
distractors.B: A MIB walk retrieves a tree of OIDs on demand — still manager-initiated, not event-driven.
distractors.C: Syslog facility codes categorize log sources; they are not an SNMP notification mechanism.

explanation.exam_pattern: Trap/inform = agent pushes an event to the manager; GET/poll = manager pulls on a schedule.

questions.stem: While correlating syslog entries from many devices during an incident, the analyst finds the timestamps don't line up, making it impossible to order events. Which service should be deployed to fix this?

options.text: NTP to synchronize device clocks to a common time source
A higher minimum syslog severity level

explanation.correct: Correlatable, orderable log timestamps require every device to share the same accurate clock, so all devices should sync to a common NTP time source.

distractors.B: DHCP scope size has nothing to do with the accuracy or alignment of log timestamps.
distractors.C: Severity level only filters which messages are logged; it does not align clocks.
distractors.D: SNMPv3 secures SNMP; it does not synchronize time for log timestamps.

explanation.exam_pattern: Consistent, correlatable log timestamps across devices = NTP (sync all devices to the same time source).

questions.stem: In SNMP, a manager retrieves a value identified by a hierarchical numeric string (for example 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 for system uptime). What is this identifier called, and where is its definition stored?

options.text: A syslog facility, stored on the resolver
An OID, defined in a MIB
A community string, stored on the agent
A trap, stored on the manager

explanation.correct: The dotted-number string is an Object Identifier (OID) that uniquely addresses a managed object; the MIB is the database/definitions that describe those objects and their OIDs.

distractors.A: A syslog facility categorizes log messages and is unrelated to SNMP object naming.
distractors.C: A community string is the shared password used by SNMP v1/v2c, not an object identifier.
distractors.D: A trap is an unsolicited event notification, not the identifier of a polled value.

explanation.exam_pattern: MIB = the definitions/database; OID = the dotted-number address of a specific object; agent holds values, manager queries them.

questions.stem: A network team needs a AAA protocol for device administration that encrypts the ENTIRE packet payload and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting so individual CLI commands can be authorized per administrator. Which protocol BEST fits?

explanation.correct: TACACS+ (TCP 49) encrypts the full packet body and treats authentication, authorization, and accounting as independent functions, which is why it is preferred for device administration and granular per-command authorization.

distractors.A: Kerberos is a ticket-based SSO authentication system, not a device-administration AAA protocol with per-command authorization.
distractors.C: LDAP queries a directory for identity/attribute lookups; it is not an AAA protocol that authorizes administrative commands.
distractors.D: RADIUS encrypts only the password in the Access-Request (not the whole packet), combines authentication and authorization, and uses UDP; it is common for network access (e.g., 802.1X) rather than per-command device admin.

explanation.exam_pattern: Encrypts the whole packet + separates A/A/A + per-command device admin = TACACS+ (TCP 49). Encrypts only the password + combines authn/authz + UDP = RADIUS.

questions.stem: A security architecture assumes NO device or user is trusted by default — even on the internal LAN — and continuously verifies identity and posture for every access request before granting the minimum access needed. Which concept is being described?

options.text: Implicit trust based on network location

explanation.correct: Zero trust removes implicit trust tied to network location and requires continuous verification (identity, device posture, policy) for every request, granting only least-privilege access — 'never trust, always verify.'

distractors.B: Defense in depth layers multiple controls, but it does not by itself mandate per-request verification with no implicit trust; it is a complementary idea, not the one described.
distractors.C: Trusting a host simply because it sits inside the perimeter is exactly the legacy model zero trust replaces.
distractors.D: A screened subnet (DMZ) is a segmentation zone for public-facing servers, not an access-trust model.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Never trust, always verify,' no trust by location, continuous verification + least privilege = zero trust.

questions.stem: Near a company office, an attacker stands up a wireless access point broadcasting the SAME SSID as the corporate WLAN, hoping employee devices associate to it so their traffic can be intercepted. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: An evil twin is a malicious access point that impersonates a legitimate SSID so victims connect to it, letting the attacker capture or manipulate their traffic.

distractors.A: A deauthentication attack sends spoofed 802.11 deauth frames to knock clients off a network; it can precede an evil twin but is not the impersonating AP itself.
distractors.B: DNS poisoning corrupts name-resolution responses to redirect by hostname, not by spoofing a Wi-Fi SSID.
distractors.D: A rogue DHCP server hands out malicious IP configuration on a wired/wireless segment; it does not impersonate an SSID to lure associations.

explanation.exam_pattern: Malicious AP broadcasting a legitimate SSID to lure clients = evil twin.

questions.stem: From an access port in VLAN 10, an attacker crafts a frame with TWO stacked 802.1Q tags. The first switch strips the outer (native VLAN) tag and forwards the frame on a trunk; the inner tag then steers it into VLAN 20, which the attacker should not reach. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: Double-tagging VLAN hopping abuses the native VLAN: the first switch removes the outer tag and the remaining inner tag delivers the frame into a VLAN the attacker is not a member of.

distractors.A: DHCP starvation exhausts a DHCP scope with spoofed requests; it is an availability attack on addressing, not VLAN traversal.
distractors.C: ARP spoofing forges IP-to-MAC bindings for on-path interception, operating within a VLAN rather than hopping between VLANs via tagging.
distractors.D: MAC flooding overwhelms the switch CAM table to force unknown-unicast flooding; it does not use stacked tags to cross VLANs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stacked 802.1Q tags exploiting the native VLAN = double-tagging VLAN hopping. Mitigate by assigning the native VLAN to an unused VLAN and disabling auto-trunking.

questions.stem: A company hosts public web and email servers that Internet users must reach, but it does NOT want inbound Internet traffic to touch the internal LAN. Where should these servers be placed?

options.text: On the internal user LAN alongside workstations
In a screened subnet (DMZ) between the Internet and the internal network
Directly on the Internet with public IPs and no firewall

explanation.correct: A screened subnet (DMZ) is an isolated segment for public-facing servers: firewall policy permits the needed inbound traffic to the DMZ while blocking that traffic from reaching the trusted internal LAN.

distractors.A: Placing public servers on the internal LAN exposes workstations and internal resources to Internet-originated traffic — the opposite of the requirement.
distractors.C: The out-of-band management network is a protected admin-only path for managing devices, not a place to publish public services.
distractors.D: Putting servers directly on the Internet with no firewall removes all protection and segmentation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Public-facing servers reachable from the Internet but isolated from the LAN = screened subnet (DMZ).

questions.stem: Clients on an access switch intermittently receive IP addresses and a default gateway from an unauthorized device plugged into a user port. The admin wants the switch to accept DHCP server replies (OFFER/ACK) ONLY from the uplink toward the real DHCP server and drop them on all user ports. Which feature does this?

explanation.correct: DHCP snooping marks ports as trusted or untrusted; DHCP server messages are permitted only on trusted ports (the legitimate uplink) and dropped on untrusted user ports, defeating rogue DHCP servers. It also builds a binding table of IP-to-MAC/port.

distractors.A: BPDU guard protects spanning tree by disabling a port that receives unexpected BPDUs; it is unrelated to DHCP.
distractors.B: Dynamic ARP inspection validates ARP packets against the snooping binding table; it mitigates ARP spoofing, not rogue DHCP replies.
distractors.D: Port security restricts which MAC addresses may use a port; it does not distinguish legitimate from rogue DHCP server traffic.

explanation.exam_pattern: Block rogue DHCP by trusting only the real server's port = DHCP snooping (it also feeds the binding table used by DAI and IP Source Guard).

questions.stem: After an ARP spoofing incident, a network engineer wants switches to intercept ARP packets on untrusted ports and DROP any whose IP-to-MAC binding does not match a known-good table. Which feature provides this, and what does it depend on?

options.text: An extended ACL applied to the SVI
Dynamic ARP inspection, using the DHCP snooping binding table
Port security with sticky MAC learning

explanation.correct: Dynamic ARP inspection (DAI) validates each ARP packet on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table (or static ARP ACLs) and discards packets with a forged IP-to-MAC mapping, stopping ARP spoofing/poisoning.

distractors.A: An ACL filters IP traffic by addresses/ports/protocols; ARP is a Layer 2 protocol that standard/extended IP ACLs do not evaluate.
distractors.C: Port security limits MAC addresses per port; it does not verify the IP-to-MAC binding carried inside ARP messages.
distractors.D: DHCP snooping builds the binding table DAI relies on but does not itself inspect or drop ARP packets.

explanation.exam_pattern: Drop forged ARP by checking the IP-to-MAC binding = Dynamic ARP Inspection, which depends on the DHCP snooping binding table.

questions.stem: To remotely manage switches and routers over an ENCRYPTED session and eliminate clear-text credentials crossing the network, an administrator should disable Telnet and enable which protocol?

explanation.correct: SSH (TCP 22) encrypts the entire management session, including credentials, and is the secure replacement for Telnet, which sends everything in clear text.

distractors.A: Changing Telnet's port does not add encryption — the session is still clear text and credentials remain exposed.
distractors.B: SNMPv2c is a monitoring protocol and uses clear-text community strings; it is not an encrypted interactive management session and does not replace Telnet.
distractors.C: HTTP is a clear-text management/web protocol; HTTPS would be the encrypted option, not HTTP.

explanation.exam_pattern: Replace clear-text Telnet (TCP 23) with encrypted SSH (TCP 22) for device management.

questions.stem: A technician is hardening a newly installed access switch before connecting it to the production network. Which TWO actions are hardening best practices? (Choose two.)

options.text: Leave every port in the default VLAN 1 for simplicity
Enable Telnet so remote access is easier
Configure SNMPv1 with the community string 'public'
Change the default administrator username and password

explanation.correct: Replacing default credentials removes a well-known, easily guessed entry point, and disabling unused ports shrinks the attack surface so an intruder cannot simply plug in to an open live port.

distractors.B: Leaving hosts in VLAN 1 (the default/native VLAN) is discouraged; unused ports and the native VLAN should be moved off VLAN 1 to limit exposure.
distractors.C: Telnet is clear text; enabling it weakens the device — SSH should be used instead.
distractors.D: SNMPv1 with the default 'public' community sends clear-text, well-known credentials; SNMPv3 (authenticated/encrypted) is the hardened choice.

explanation.exam_pattern: New-device hardening staples: change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH/SNMPv3, and avoid default VLAN 1.

questions.stem: A design requires that administrators can still reach device consoles to manage and recover equipment even when the production data network is saturated or down. Management traffic rides a separate, dedicated path via console/management ports. What is this approach called?

explanation.correct: Out-of-band management uses a separate, dedicated channel (console servers, dedicated management ports, sometimes a cellular/modem path) so devices remain reachable even if the production network is unavailable.

distractors.A: Port mirroring (SPAN) copies traffic to a monitoring port for analysis; it is not a management access method.
distractors.B: In-band management shares the production data network — exactly what fails when that network is down or congested.
distractors.C: Split tunneling is a VPN client setting that sends only some traffic through the tunnel; it is unrelated to a dedicated management path.

explanation.exam_pattern: Separate dedicated path that works when the data network is down = out-of-band management; sharing the production network = in-band.

questions.stem: A company wants to permanently link the LANs of its headquarters and a branch office across the Internet so hosts at both sites communicate as if on one network. The tunnel is terminated by each site's edge firewall/router, not by individual user devices. Which solution is this?

options.text: A host-to-host (transport-mode) tunnel between two servers

explanation.correct: A site-to-site VPN joins two networks through a persistent tunnel between their edge gateways; end hosts need no VPN software because the gateways encrypt/decrypt on their behalf.

distractors.A: A host-to-host tunnel secures traffic between two specific endpoints, not the full LANs behind two gateways.
distractors.C: A clientless SSL VPN gives an individual user browser-based access to specific apps — it does not bridge two site LANs.
distractors.D: A client-to-site VPN connects a single user's device into the network, not two whole LANs via their gateways.

explanation.exam_pattern: Two whole sites joined gateway-to-gateway = site-to-site VPN; a single user's device dialing in = client-to-site.

questions.stem: A remote-access VPN is configured for SPLIT tunneling. Which TWO statements correctly describe its behavior? (Choose two.)

options.text: Split tunneling blocks the client from reaching any local LAN device such as a home printer.
Split tunneling encrypts the client's traffic at the physical layer.
Traffic destined for corporate subnets is sent through the encrypted VPN tunnel.
All client traffic, including general web browsing, is forced through the corporate network for inspection.
Internet-bound traffic leaves the client's local connection without traversing the corporate gateway.

explanation.correct: With split tunneling, only traffic bound for corporate resources is routed into the encrypted tunnel; everything else (general Internet traffic) exits the client's local connection directly, reducing load on the corporate gateway.

distractors.A: Split tunneling actually allows reaching local LAN devices, since local/Internet traffic is not pulled into the tunnel.
distractors.B: VPNs protect traffic with encryption at Layer 3 (e.g., IPsec) or the session layer (SSL/TLS), not at the physical layer.
distractors.D: Forcing ALL traffic through the corporate gateway describes FULL tunneling, the opposite of split tunneling.

explanation.exam_pattern: Split tunnel = corporate traffic in the tunnel, Internet traffic direct. Full tunnel = everything through the corporate gateway.

questions.stem: In an IPsec VPN, which component provides CONFIDENTIALITY by encrypting the packet payload (in addition to integrity and authentication)?

explanation.correct: ESP (IP protocol 50) encrypts the payload to provide confidentiality, and can also provide integrity and authentication — it is the IPsec component that actually encrypts the data.

distractors.B: GRE is a tunneling/encapsulation protocol with no built-in encryption; it needs IPsec to add confidentiality.
distractors.C: AH (IP protocol 51) provides integrity and authentication only; it does NOT encrypt the payload, so it offers no confidentiality.
distractors.D: IKE (UDP 500/4500) negotiates the security associations and keys; it sets up the tunnel but is not what encrypts the ongoing data payload.

explanation.exam_pattern: Encryption/confidentiality in IPsec = ESP. AH = integrity/authentication only (no encryption). IKE = key exchange / SA negotiation.

questions.stem: A help-desk technician needs to connect to the full graphical desktop of a remote Windows server to run GUI management tools. Which native Microsoft protocol and port are used?

explanation.correct: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is Microsoft's native remote-GUI protocol and listens on TCP 3389.

distractors.A: SSH (TCP 22) provides an encrypted command-line session, typically to Linux/Unix hosts and network devices — not a Windows graphical desktop.
distractors.C: VNC does offer a remote GUI and uses TCP 5900, but it is a cross-platform third-party protocol, not Microsoft's native protocol, and it is not on 3389.
distractors.D: Telnet (TCP 23) is an unencrypted text/CLI protocol, not a graphical remote desktop.

explanation.exam_pattern: Windows remote graphical desktop = RDP, TCP 3389. SSH 22 = secure CLI; VNC 5900 = cross-platform GUI; Telnet 23 = clear-text CLI.

questions.stem: To administer servers in a protected subnet, administrators must first connect to a single hardened host positioned between the admin network and the secure zone; all management sessions are funneled and logged through it. What is this host called?

explanation.correct: A jump box (bastion host) is a single hardened, closely monitored system used as the controlled entry point for administering devices in a secure zone, concentrating and logging all management access.

distractors.A: A RADIUS server performs AAA for network access; it authenticates users but is not the pivot host through which admins connect.
distractors.B: A forward proxy relays user requests (typically outbound web traffic) on their behalf; it is not a hardened administrative pivot host.
distractors.C: A honeypot is a decoy system meant to attract and study attackers, not a sanctioned admin gateway.

explanation.exam_pattern: Single hardened pivot/entry host for reaching a secure zone = jump box / bastion host.

questions.stem: A server-room door is secured with a fingerprint scanner, so entry depends on a physical trait that cannot be lost, shared, or easily duplicated. This access control is BEST described as which authentication factor?

options.text: Asset tag — something you are assigned

explanation.correct: A fingerprint (or retina/face) scanner is biometric authentication — the 'something you are' factor — tied to a unique physical trait that cannot be handed to someone else.

distractors.A: A PIN or cipher-lock code is 'something you know' and can be shared or shoulder-surfed.
distractors.B: A proximity card is 'something you have'; it can be lost, stolen, or cloned, so it is not the trait-based factor described.
distractors.D: An asset tag labels equipment for inventory; it is not a personal authentication factor at all.

explanation.exam_pattern: Fingerprint/retina/face at a door = biometric, the 'something you are' factor.

questions.stem: Management wants to continuously monitor and RECORD who is physically present at the data center entrances so any incident can be reviewed afterward. Which physical security control BEST meets this need?

explanation.correct: Security cameras (CCTV) continuously capture and store video of entrances, providing a detective record that can be reviewed after an incident (and a visible deterrent).

distractors.A: Motion-activated lighting improves visibility and deters intruders but records nothing for later review.
distractors.B: Bollards block vehicles from an entrance; they neither monitor nor record people.
distractors.C: An access control vestibule prevents tailgating by admitting one person at a time, but it does not create a reviewable visual record of who was present.

explanation.exam_pattern: Continuously record/monitor who is present for later review = security cameras (CCTV).

questions.stem: A facility wants to stop a vehicle from being driven through the glass doors of its lobby entrance while still allowing pedestrians to walk through. Which physical control is MOST appropriate?

explanation.correct: Bollards are short, sturdy posts set in front of an entrance to physically block vehicles from ramming through while still letting people walk between them.

distractors.A: Perimeter fencing marks and deters access at the property boundary but is not what protects a specific pedestrian doorway from a vehicle.
distractors.B: An access control vestibule controls people tailgating through a door — it is not designed to stop a vehicle.
distractors.C: Security lighting improves visibility and deters intruders; it provides no physical barrier to a vehicle.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stop a vehicle at an entrance while allowing foot traffic = bollards.

questions.stem: An IT department attaches scannable RFID/barcode labels to every switch, router, and laptop so equipment can be inventoried and, if it leaves the building, identified as company property. What are these labels called?

explanation.correct: Asset tags are labels (often RFID or barcode) applied to equipment for inventory tracking and to mark ownership, aiding accountability and theft identification.

distractors.A: Smart lockers securely store or hand off devices/packages; they are not labels affixed to equipment.
distractors.B: Tamper-evident seals reveal whether a device has been opened or tampered with — a different purpose from inventory/ownership tracking.
distractors.C: Proximity badges authenticate people at doors; they do not inventory equipment.

explanation.exam_pattern: Labels for inventory and ownership tracking of equipment = asset tags.

questions.stem: A company wants to know whether anyone has physically OPENED the chassis of a deployed network appliance in a remote closet. Which control BEST provides this?

options.text: A proximity card reader on the closet door

explanation.correct: Tamper detection — tamper-evident seals or tamper switches/sensors — makes unauthorized opening of a device visible or logs it, so technicians can tell the chassis was accessed.

distractors.A: A card reader controls who enters the closet; it does not detect tampering with the device itself once someone is inside.
distractors.B: An asset tag identifies ownership and aids inventory; it does not indicate whether the device was opened.
distractors.D: A cable lock deters theft of the device but does not reveal that the chassis was opened.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reveal that a device chassis was opened = tamper detection (seals/sensors).

questions.stem: A ticket states only 'the internet is down.' Before changing anything, the technician interviews the user, asks what recently changed, and tries to reproduce the failure. Which step of the CompTIA methodology is this?

options.text: Establish a theory of probable cause
Test the theory to determine the cause

explanation.correct: Step 1, identify the problem, is where you gather information, question users, determine what changed, and duplicate the problem if possible.

distractors.B: Establishing a theory (step 2) comes only after you have identified and scoped the problem.
distractors.C: Testing the theory (step 3) requires a theory to test, which does not exist yet.
distractors.D: Verifying full functionality (step 6) happens after a fix is implemented.

explanation.exam_pattern: Gather info / question users / ask what changed / duplicate = Step 1, Identify the problem.

questions.stem: A technician has implemented a fix and the application now responds. According to the CompTIA methodology, what should be done BEFORE documenting the outcome?

options.text: Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, implement preventive measures
Escalate the issue to the vendor
Identify the problem and question users
Establish a theory of probable cause

explanation.correct: Step 6 is verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures; documentation (step 7) is the final step, after verification.

distractors.B: Escalation belongs to step 5 (implement the solution OR escalate), not after a successful fix.
distractors.C: Identifying the problem is step 1, the very beginning of the process.
distractors.D: Establishing a theory is step 2, long before a fix is implemented.

explanation.exam_pattern: After the fix, VERIFY (step 6) before you DOCUMENT (step 7).

questions.stem: While testing a theory of probable cause, the technician proves the theory is wrong. According to the CompTIA methodology, what is the correct NEXT action?

options.text: Implement the original solution anyway and watch for results
Document that the problem cannot be solved
Establish a new theory or escalate

explanation.correct: If testing does not confirm the theory, the methodology says to establish a new theory (reattempt step 2) or escalate to someone with more expertise.

distractors.A: Implementing a fix for a disproven theory is premature; you have not found the cause.
distractors.B: Verification occurs only after a solution has actually been implemented.
distractors.C: A disproven theory does not mean the problem is unsolvable; you form another theory.

explanation.exam_pattern: Theory confirmed -> plan/implement. Theory NOT confirmed -> new theory or escalate.

questions.stem: When establishing a theory of probable cause, a technician deliberately begins at Layer 1 (check the cable and link) and works upward through the OSI model. What is this approach called?

explanation.correct: Starting at the physical layer and moving up toward the application layer is the bottom-to-top (bottom-up) OSI troubleshooting approach.

distractors.B: Divide and conquer starts at a middle layer and moves up or down based on results.
distractors.C: Top-to-bottom starts at the application layer and works DOWN toward the physical layer.
distractors.D: Escalation is handing the issue to higher-tier support, not an OSI testing strategy.

explanation.exam_pattern: Layer 1 upward = bottom-to-top; Layer 7 downward = top-to-bottom; start in the middle = divide and conquer.

questions.stem: Which activities belong to Step 1, 'Identify the problem,' of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology? (Choose two.)

options.text: Determine whether anything has recently changed
Submit a final root-cause report to management
Question users and gather information about the symptoms

explanation.correct: Step 1 includes gathering information, questioning users, identifying symptoms, determining if anything changed, and duplicating the problem if possible.

distractors.B: Reporting/documenting findings and outcomes is step 7, the final step.
distractors.C: Implementing preventive measures is part of step 6 (verify full system functionality).

explanation.exam_pattern: Identify the problem = ask users, find symptoms, ask what changed, duplicate the issue.

questions.stem: A copper patch cable passes a basic wiremap/continuity test showing all eight pins connected end-to-end, yet gigabit links on it suffer excessive crosstalk and errors. Which wiring fault is MOST likely?

explanation.correct: Split pairs keep correct pin-to-pin continuity (so a basic wiremap tester passes) but break the twisted-pair pairing, so near-end crosstalk (NEXT) rises and high-speed links fail. A cable certifier is needed to detect it.

distractors.B: A distance problem is a loss/attenuation issue unrelated to a cable that tests continuous but has high crosstalk.
distractors.C: An open conductor breaks continuity on that pin, so a wiremap tester would flag it, not pass.
distractors.D: A short also fails the continuity test and typically shows as connected pins that should not be.

explanation.exam_pattern: Continuity test PASSES but crosstalk is high = split pairs (only a certifier catches it).

questions.stem: An uplink between two switches uses single-mode (SMF) transceivers, but a technician patches it with multimode (MMF) fiber jumpers. The link will not come up or shows very high optical loss. What is the problem?

options.text: The jumpers are too short for the transceivers
Auto-MDIX is disabled on the switches
The transceivers need a crossover adapter
Fiber type mismatch - single-mode optics require single-mode fiber

explanation.correct: Single-mode optics are built for the ~9-micron SMF core; forcing their signal through a 50/62.5-micron multimode core causes severe loss and a failed link. Match fiber type to the optics.

distractors.A: Jumper length does not cause a type mismatch; a too-short cord simply would not reach.
distractors.B: Auto-MDIX concerns copper TX/RX crossover, not fiber-mode compatibility.
distractors.C: Crossover adapters relate to copper straight/crossover wiring, not single-mode vs multimode fiber.

explanation.exam_pattern: SMF optics + MMF cord (or vice versa) = fiber type mismatch, huge loss or no link.

questions.stem: A UTP run is bundled tightly alongside fluorescent light ballasts and power conduit. The link shows intermittent errors that get worse whenever the lights are on. Which cabling issue is this?

explanation.correct: Power conduit and fluorescent ballasts emit electromagnetic fields that induce noise into unshielded twisted pair. The correlation with the lights is the tell. Reroute with separation or use shielded cable.

distractors.A: Attenuation is signal loss over distance; it is constant and not tied to whether the lights are on.
distractors.B: A duplex mismatch causes collisions and CRC errors regardless of nearby lighting.
distractors.D: An open circuit breaks the link entirely rather than causing intermittent, light-correlated errors.

explanation.exam_pattern: Errors that track with nearby power/lighting = EMI; separate cables or use STP.

questions.stem: A fiber link that worked at install begins showing increased optical loss and intermittent errors after a patch cord was repeatedly unplugged and reseated. Inspection shows contamination on the ferrule end-face. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Increase the MTU on both ends
Clean the fiber connector end-faces with proper fiber-cleaning tools

explanation.correct: A dirty fiber connector is one of the most common causes of optical loss. Inspecting and cleaning the end-face with the correct tools restores the link before considering hardware swaps.

distractors.A: MTU affects frame size, not optical signal level on a dirty connector.
distractors.B: Duplex settings are a copper/negotiation concept and do not fix a contaminated fiber end-face.
distractors.D: A power-supply fault would not produce localized contamination-related optical loss on one link.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rising fiber loss after reseating + visible contamination = dirty connector; clean it first.

questions.stem: A patch cable was terminated with the T568A standard on one end and T568B on the other. On legacy equipment without Auto-MDIX, what is the effect of this cable?

options.text: It behaves as a crossover cable, swapping the transmit and receive pairs
It creates a short across all four pairs
It converts the copper link into single-mode fiber

explanation.correct: Mixing T568A on one end with T568B on the other swaps pairs 2 and 3, which produces a crossover cable - transmit and receive are crossed. Without Auto-MDIX that is wrong for a host-to-switch run.

distractors.B: Pinout has nothing to do with cable length or the 100-meter channel limit.
distractors.C: Different termination standards do not short conductors together; each pin still maps to one pin.
distractors.D: Termination standards apply to copper; they cannot turn a cable into fiber.

explanation.exam_pattern: T568A on one end + T568B on the other = a crossover (TX/RX swapped).

questions.stem: A long-haul fiber link has failed, and the technician needs to find the distance to a break or high-loss event along the fiber. Which tool is designed for this?

explanation.correct: An OTDR sends light pulses down the fiber and times the reflected light, mapping splices, bends, and breaks and reporting the distance to each event.

distractors.A: A multimeter measures electrical values (voltage/resistance), not optical fiber faults.
distractors.B: A tone generator and probe traces copper cables, not faults on fiber.
distractors.D: A loopback plug tests a local port or interface; it cannot locate a fiber break by distance.

explanation.exam_pattern: Distance-to-fault on fiber = OTDR.

questions.stem: A technician suspects a fiber link's received signal is too weak and wants to measure the actual received optical power in dBm to compare against the transceiver's power budget. Which tool should be used?

explanation.correct: An optical power meter reads absolute received power in dBm at a point, which is exactly what you compare to the transceiver's receive-sensitivity budget.

distractors.A: A protocol analyzer decodes captured packets; it has no visibility into optical power levels.
distractors.C: A copper cable certifier measures twisted-pair parameters and cannot read optical power.
distractors.D: An OTDR characterizes the fiber and locates events via backscatter; it is not the simple end-to-end dBm power reading.

explanation.exam_pattern: Read received optical power in dBm = optical power/light meter; find the fault location = OTDR.

questions.stem: Users in one area report slow, dropping Wi-Fi, and the technician suspects nearby access points are using overlapping 2.4 GHz channels. Which tool BEST confirms channel usage and overlap?

explanation.correct: A Wi-Fi analyzer shows which channels nearby SSIDs occupy, their signal strength, and overlap, letting you pick non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11 in 2.4 GHz).

distractors.A: A tone generator and probe traces physical copper cables, not wireless channels.
distractors.C: A loopback plug tests a wired port, not wireless spectrum usage.
distractors.D: A copper cable tester checks wired continuity/wiremap, irrelevant to RF channel overlap.

explanation.exam_pattern: Channel overlap / interference / signal strength survey = Wi-Fi analyzer.

questions.stem: An application intermittently fails, and the team must inspect the actual packets, TCP handshakes, and retransmissions on the wire to find the cause. Which tool is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A protocol analyzer / packet capture (e.g., Wireshark or tcpdump)

explanation.correct: A protocol analyzer captures and decodes frames so you can inspect the three-way handshake, retransmissions, resets, and application payloads to pinpoint the failure.

distractors.B: A cable certifier validates physical cabling, not protocol-level conversations.
distractors.C: ping only confirms reachability and round-trip time; it does not decode application traffic.
distractors.D: ipconfig /all shows the local IP configuration, not packets on the wire.

explanation.exam_pattern: Need to see the actual packets / handshake / retransmissions = protocol analyzer (packet capture).

questions.stem: Traffic to a remote site is slow, and a technician wants per-hop latency AND packet loss sampled over time to find which hop introduces delay. On Windows, which tool provides this combined per-hop data?

explanation.correct: pathping combines the functions of ping and tracert, sending probes over a sampling period to report per-hop latency and packet-loss percentages along the path.

distractors.A: arp -a displays the local IP-to-MAC cache, not path statistics.
distractors.B: netstat -r prints the local routing table, not live per-hop latency and loss.
distractors.D: nslookup queries DNS name resolution; it does not measure per-hop latency or loss.

explanation.exam_pattern: Per-hop latency + loss over time on Windows = pathping (ping + tracert combined).

questions.stem: A technician needs to view a workstation's current IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway. Which commands display this LOCAL interface configuration? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: ipconfig /all (Windows) and ip address / ifconfig (Linux/Unix) print the adapter's IP, mask, gateway, and DNS settings assigned to the local host.

distractors.C: nslookup queries DNS for name resolution; it does not show the local adapter's configuration.
distractors.D: tracert maps the path to a destination; it does not list the local IP/mask/gateway settings.

explanation.exam_pattern: Show local IP config: ipconfig (Windows) and ip/ifconfig (Linux).

questions.stem: After an employee plugged a consumer wireless router into a wall jack, some clients began leasing addresses in an unexpected range with a wrong default gateway and lost access to corporate resources. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The clients fell back to APIPA
DNS cache poisoning on the corporate DNS server
A duplex mismatch on the uplink
A rogue DHCP server is handing out incorrect leases

explanation.correct: The consumer router runs its own DHCP service; clients that lease from it get the router's range and gateway instead of the corporate ones. DHCP snooping prevents rogue servers.

distractors.A: APIPA (169.254.x.x) only appears when NO DHCP answers; here clients did receive leases, just from the wrong server.
distractors.B: DNS poisoning corrupts name-to-IP answers; it does not change a client's leased IP/gateway range.
distractors.C: A duplex mismatch causes errors and slowness, not clients leasing addresses from the wrong range.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unauthorized device leasing wrong IP/gateway = rogue DHCP; mitigate with DHCP snooping.

questions.stem: A host is set to IP 10.1.5.20 with mask 255.255.255.0 and gateway 10.1.4.1. It can reach other hosts in 10.1.5.0/24 but cannot reach its gateway or any remote network. What is the cause?

options.text: An expired TLS certificate on the gateway
An incorrect subnet mask - the gateway is outside the host's configured subnet
A rogue access point on the LAN

explanation.correct: With a /24 mask the host treats only 10.1.5.0-10.1.5.255 as local, so gateway 10.1.4.1 looks unreachable and all off-subnet traffic fails. A /23 mask (255.255.254.0) would include the gateway.

distractors.A: A TLS certificate affects HTTPS trust, not IP-layer reachability of a gateway.
distractors.C: A statically or correctly leased address still works locally; an exhausted scope would stop new leases, not break routing like this.
distractors.D: A rogue AP is a wireless security concern and does not explain a mask/gateway mismatch.

explanation.exam_pattern: Local works, remote fails, gateway unreachable = wrong subnet mask putting the gateway off-subnet.

questions.stem: Two devices on the same LAN intermittently lose connectivity, and one displays an 'IP address conflict' message. A static IP had been configured inside the active DHCP range. What is the cause?

options.text: A duplicate IP address - the static address overlaps a DHCP-assigned lease

explanation.correct: Assigning a static IP inside the DHCP pool (without an exclusion or reservation) lets DHCP hand the same address to another host, producing a duplicate-IP conflict and intermittent loss.

distractors.A: An MTU mismatch causes drops of large frames, not an IP-address-conflict notification.
distractors.B: An SPF record is an email anti-spoofing DNS record, unrelated to IP conflicts.
distractors.C: APIPA uses 169.254.x.x when no DHCP answers; it does not produce a conflict message between two devices.

explanation.exam_pattern: Static IP inside the DHCP range = duplicate IP / address conflict; exclude or reserve it.

questions.stem: Users cannot reach internal servers by name, but connecting by IP address works. The technician finds the clients' configured DNS server is an address that was decommissioned last week. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Point the clients at a valid DNS server (correct the DHCP option 6 or static entry)
Replace the Ethernet cabling to the clients
Enable jumbo frames on the clients

explanation.correct: Working by IP but failing by name is a name-resolution (DNS) problem. The clients point at a dead DNS server, so correct the DNS server address they are given (DHCP option 6 or static).

distractors.B: Lease duration governs how long an address is held; it does not repair a bad DNS server setting.
distractors.C: Cabling is fine - IP connectivity works - so re-cabling does not fix name resolution.
distractors.D: Jumbo frames change MTU; they have no effect on DNS name resolution.

explanation.exam_pattern: Works by IP, fails by name = DNS; fix the DNS server the clients are configured to use.

questions.stem: A new internal web app is unreachable on TCP 443 from a branch office, yet the same clients successfully ping the server by IP, and other internal sites work. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: A firewall or ACL along the path is blocking TCP 443
The server NIC is stuck in half-duplex

explanation.correct: ICMP ping succeeds (reachability and routing are fine) but the specific TCP port fails - the classic signature of a firewall rule or ACL blocking that port/service along the path.

distractors.B: With APIPA (169.254.x.x) the clients could not ping the server or reach other sites at all.
distractors.C: An exhausted DHCP scope prevents getting an address; these clients clearly have working IP connectivity.
distractors.D: A duplex problem degrades all traffic with errors; it would not block only TCP 443 while ping works.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ping works but a specific port/service fails = blocked port (firewall/ACL).

questions.stem: Users report choppy, robotic VoIP audio during busy periods, though data apps are fine. Monitoring shows highly variable packet delay on the voice stream. Which action BEST addresses this?

options.text: Disable Auto-MDIX on the access switches
Implement QoS to prioritize voice traffic (and use a jitter buffer)

explanation.correct: Variable delay is jitter, which wrecks real-time voice. QoS prioritizes/queues voice ahead of bulk data, and a jitter buffer smooths the variation, restoring clear audio.

distractors.A: DHCP lease time governs addressing, not real-time voice delay variation.
distractors.B: Auto-MDIX concerns cable TX/RX detection and has nothing to do with voice jitter.
distractors.D: DNS resolves names; it does not affect jitter on an established call.

explanation.exam_pattern: Choppy VoIP + variable delay = jitter; fix with QoS prioritization and a jitter buffer.

questions.stem: A switch interface counter shows a rising number of 'giants.' What does this counter indicate?

options.text: Frames received that are larger than the maximum allowed frame size
The total count of broadcast frames
Jumbo frames that were successfully forwarded

explanation.correct: Giants are frames that exceed the maximum allowed size (e.g., beyond the configured MTU), often from a faulty NIC/driver or an MTU/jumbo misconfiguration.

distractors.A: Frames smaller than 64 bytes are runts, usually from collisions or a bad NIC - the opposite of giants.
distractors.C: Broadcasts are tracked separately and are not what the giants counter measures.
distractors.D: The giants counter flags oversized/error frames, not successfully forwarded jumbo frames.

explanation.exam_pattern: Giants = oversized frames; runts = undersized (<64 byte) frames.

questions.stem: A WAN link's utilization graph sits at 100% every afternoon, and throughput-sensitive applications slow for all users during those hours. What does this MOST likely indicate?

explanation.correct: Sustained 100% utilization means the link is saturated; queued and dropped packets slow everyone. Remedies include more bandwidth or QoS/traffic shaping to protect priority traffic.

distractors.A: An expired/exhausted DHCP scope blocks new leases; it does not drive link utilization to 100%.
distractors.B: A DNS problem breaks name resolution; it does not peg a link at 100% utilization.
distractors.D: A duplicate IP affects two specific hosts intermittently, not a time-of-day full-link saturation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Link pinned at 100% utilization + slowness for all = bandwidth saturation/congestion.

questions.stem: After jumbo frames (MTU 9000) were enabled on some servers and storage but an intermediate switch was left at 1500, large transfers fail or perform terribly while small pings succeed. What is the cause?

options.text: A duplex mismatch on the uplink
An MTU (jumbo-frame) mismatch along the path

explanation.correct: Jumbo frames must be enabled end-to-end. A device left at 1500 drops the oversized frames (or forces fragmentation), so small packets pass but large transfers fail. Match MTU across the whole path.

distractors.A: A dirty fiber connector raises optical loss for all traffic, not selectively for large frames.
distractors.B: A duplex mismatch produces collisions/CRC errors on all traffic, not a clean small-works/large-fails pattern.
distractors.D: A rogue DHCP server affects addressing, not frame-size handling of large transfers.

explanation.exam_pattern: Small packets fine, large fail across a path = MTU/jumbo-frame mismatch; set MTU consistently end-to-end.

questions.stem: A core router becomes sluggish, drops packets, and responds slowly to management sessions. Monitoring shows its CPU pegged near 100% during a traffic spike. Which performance issue is this?

options.text: An incorrect subnet mask on the clients

explanation.correct: When a device's CPU or memory is exhausted it cannot process or forward traffic promptly, so it drops packets and responds slowly regardless of link health. Investigate the process/traffic, then offload or upgrade.

distractors.A: A split-pair fault causes crosstalk on a cable run, not device-wide CPU exhaustion.
distractors.B: An incorrect subnet mask breaks specific hosts' routing, not the router's CPU utilization.
distractors.D: Attenuation is a cabling/signal-loss issue on one link; it would not peg the router's CPU.

explanation.exam_pattern: Device slow + drops + CPU/memory near 100% = resource exhaustion on the device itself.
